content.value_statement: Plain text logs are hard to search and correlate. This skill helps implement JSON logging, request context, redaction, and aggregation-ready fields.
actual_capabilities: Explains when to use fatal, error, warn, info, debug, and trace levels.
Defines common JSON log fields such as timestamp, level, message, requestId, userId, service, and environment.
Shows Node.js logger setup patterns for Pino and Winston.
Describes request ID propagation and AsyncLocalStorage request context.
Covers sensitive field redaction for passwords, tokens, API keys, credit cards, and authorization headers.
Outlines Elasticsearch and Datadog logging integration patterns.
limitations: It is a Markdown guide, not an installable logging library.
Examples focus on Node.js and TypeScript services.
Aggregation examples are starting points and need production configuration.
Redaction examples must be extended for each application data model.

use_cases.title: Add JSON Logging to a Service
use_cases.description: Replace plain text application logs with structured fields, consistent levels, and searchable request metadata.

use_cases.title: Standardize Service Log Fields
use_cases.description: Create shared logging conventions for service name, environment, request ID, duration, and error details.

use_cases.title: Prepare Logs for Incident Debugging
use_cases.description: Make production logs easier to filter, correlate, and route into aggregation tools during incidents.

prompt_templates.title: Add Basic JSON Logging
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the structured-logging skill to replace plain text logs in my Node.js service with JSON logs. Recommend fields and log levels.

prompt_templates.title: Add Request Context
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the structured-logging skill to design request ID propagation and contextual logger usage for this API. Include how errors should be logged.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Redaction Controls
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the structured-logging skill to review my logging plan for sensitive data exposure. Identify fields to redact and safe metadata to keep.

prompt_templates.title: Design Aggregation Integration
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the structured-logging skill to design an aggregation-ready logging architecture for Pino or Winston. Include Elasticsearch or Datadog considerations.

output_examples.input: A service logs plain text messages and cannot filter errors by request.
output_examples.output: A logging plan with structured fields, level guidance, and request identifiers for correlation.

output_examples.input: A payment workflow logs useful events but may expose sensitive data.
output_examples.output: A redaction checklist, safe business event fields, and warnings about fields that should never be logged.

output_examples.input: A team wants logs ready for Datadog or Elasticsearch.
output_examples.output: A provider integration outline that keeps application logs structured and searchable.

best_practices: Keep log messages short and put searchable values in structured fields.
Attach requestId and service metadata to every request-scoped log.
Redact sensitive fields before logs leave the application process.
anti_patterns: Do not log passwords, tokens, payment cards, or authorization headers.
Do not use string interpolation when fields should be searchable.
Do not emit high-volume debug logs in production by default.

faq.question: Does this skill install a logger?
faq.answer: No. It guides an agent or developer through implementing logging in an existing project.

faq.question: Which logging libraries does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers Pino and Winston examples for Node.js and TypeScript applications.

faq.question: Can it help with Datadog or Elasticsearch?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes basic integration patterns and fields that aggregation tools can index.

faq.question: Does it prevent all secret leakage?
faq.answer: No. It provides redaction patterns, but teams must define every sensitive field for their own application.

faq.question: Is it only for production systems?
faq.answer: No. It also explains development log levels and readable local output.

faq.question: Can Claude, Codex, or Claude Code use it?
faq.answer: Yes. The guidance is compatible with Claude, Codex, and Claude Code workflows.
